study.title: Massive Galaxy Halos Contain Less Inner Dark Matter Than Predicted

cover.headline: The centres of massive galaxy halos hold **less dark matter than simulations predict** in this early analysis.

slides.title: Computer models of the universe assume dark matter settles in predictable patterns around galaxies.
slides.body:
Two major simulations, IllustrisTNG and EAGLE, both predict how much dark matter should pack into the inner regions of massive galaxy halos at a given total mass. Those predictions underpin estimates of halo structure across cosmology.

This preprint reports a mismatch. When the team reconstructed mass profiles using stellar motion, neutral hydrogen dynamics, and group-based halo masses, massive observed halos showed systematically lower inner dark-matter content than the simulations expected.

slides.title: Massive halos contained lower central dark-matter fractions than predicted, a gap of about four sigma.
slides.body:
The team combined data from MaNGA stellar kinematics, ALFALFA hydrogen measurements, and SDSS galaxy-group catalogs to map mass distribution across nearly two orders of magnitude in radius. Low-mass halos matched simulations reasonably well.

Massive halos diverged. At fixed total halo mass, the observed systems had lower dynamical masses at the hydrogen radius, lower inner dark-matter masses, and dark-matter profiles consistent with lower effective concentrations than IllustrisTNG or EAGLE predict.

slides.title: The authors suggest long-term heating from baryonic matter may have displaced dark matter more than models assume.
slides.body:
After subtracting the contribution of ordinary matter, the inferred dark-matter profiles still fit the standard NFW form, but the effective concentrations were lower in massive systems. That pattern is consistent with baryons heating the halo over time.

The paper also shows that hydrogen data alone do not give reliable total halo masses. The team needed independent group-based mass calibration to anchor the reconstruction, which limits how widely the method can be applied.

caveats: This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has verified the methods or conclusions yet.
The study identified a pattern in observational data, not a cause. Other astrophysical processes could also explain the mismatch.

caption: Massive galaxy halos appear to hold less dark matter in their cores than two leading cosmological simulations predict. The team combined stellar kinematics from MaNGA, neutral hydrogen dynamics from ALFALFA, and halo masses from SDSS galaxy groups to reconstruct mass profiles spanning nearly two orders of magnitude in radius. Low-mass halos matched IllustrisTNG and EAGLE predictions, but massive halos showed a roughly four-sigma deficit in central dark-matter fraction. The inferred dark-matter profiles remained consistent with the standard NFW form but at lower concentrations, pointing to stronger baryonic heating in massive systems than models currently capture. The analysis required independent group-based mass calibration because hydrogen data alone remained unreliable. Full study: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19132v1 — Send this to anyone who keeps citing IllustrisTNG mass profiles as ground truth.
